subject: maths
title: Surds & Rationalising
welcome_lead: Time to tame the square roots: simplify surds, multiply them cleanly, and rationalise denominators like a pro.
meta_desc: GCSE Maths exam-style surds — simplifying √50, multiplying surds, rationalising denominators and reciprocals.
final_note: You can simplify surds, multiply them, rationalise denominators and handle reciprocals — exam-ready!

concepts.def: A root that can't be written as an exact whole or fraction
Pull out the biggest square factor under the root
Remove the surd from the denominator of a fraction
1 divided by the number; reciprocal of 4 is 1/4

walkthroughs.body_html:
Surds follow a friendly rule: √a × √b = √(ab).

So √4 × √9 = √36 = 6. And √2 × √8 = √16 = 4.

To simplify, find the biggest square factor. √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2. √8 = √(4 × 2) = 2√2. √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2.

Examiners hate surds on the bottom of a fraction. To clean them up, multiply top and bottom by the same surd.

Example: simplify 6/√2. Multiply top and bottom by √2: (6 × √2) / (√2 × √2) = 6√2 / 2 = 3√2.

That's rationalising: the denominator is now a tidy whole number.

The reciprocal of a number is 1 divided by it. Reciprocal of 5 is 1/5. Reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2 (flip it).

A number times its reciprocal always equals 1: 5 × 1/5 = 1.

Reciprocal of √2 is 1/√2, which after rationalising becomes √2/2.

numericals.q: Rationalise 10/√5. Type the whole-number coefficient of √5 in the answer (e.g. if the answer is 4√5, type 4).

free_texts.q: Simplify √50. Write your answer in the form a√b with no spaces (e.g. 3√2).
